screens.title: Interacting with Web Services and APIs
screens.narratorSegment: Web services and APIs are the bridges that let programs speak to cloud platforms, microservices, and external tools. In this lesson you will learn the core HTTP methods used to request, create, update, and delete resources, and you will see how the requests library makes those operations concise and readable. We'll cover how to read a response: the status code that tells you success or failure, headers that carry metadata, and JSON payloads that contain the actual data. You'll also learn practical error handling patterns: setting timeouts so scripts don't hang, using raise_for_status to detect HTTP errors, and catching network exceptions. Finally, we'll look at authentication patterns such as A P I keys and basic auth, and simple session usage for repeated requests. By the end you will be able to fetch data from a test A P I, inspect the response, and safely include credentials without embedding them directly in code. Notice why each step matters: understanding status codes avoids silent failures; proper authentication prevents rejected requests; and timeouts save automation from stalling. Ready to begin exploring these key topics with examples and starter code.

Interacting with Web Services and APIs

Responses

Explore Key Topics

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives are practical skills you will practice during the chapter. First, you'll learn the meaning and appropriate use of common HTTP methods such as GET for retrieving data, POST for creating resources, PUT for updating, and DELETE for removal. We'll pair each verb with concrete examples so you can choose the right action when calling an A P I. Second, you'll use the requests library to make requests, pass JSON payloads, and inspect responses programmatically. That includes using the json parameter to serialize data and reading response. json to parse returned data. Third, you will learn to interpret HTTP status codes and response headers so you can detect success, client errors, or server errors and respond accordingly. Finally, you'll practice basic authentication patterns and safe credential handling by using headers, environment variables, or the requests auth helpers. Each objective is framed so you can immediately apply it in an automation script or debugging session.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: In practice, these learning goals translate into repeatable tasks you will perform in automation scripts. You will construct a GET request to fetch JSON, check the status code, and safely parse the payload into Python data structures. You will write a POST call with a JSON body to create a new resource and set an explicit timeout to avoid waits that never end. You will interpret common error responses, using raise_for_status to surface HTTP errors and catching exceptions like timeouts and connection errors. Finally, you will practice attaching credentials to requests either with the auth helper for basic authentication or by adding an Authorization header for token-based access. Each objective matters because automation that assumes success without checks will behave unpredictably in production. By the end you'll be able to run small scripts against test APIs and export results confidently, knowing you handled errors and kept secrets secure.

screens.title: What is a RESTful API and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: A RESTful A P I is an interface that follows representational state transfer constraints, where clients interact with server-hosted resources via standard HTTP methods. In simple terms, an A P I exposes endpoints that represent data or services; you make requests and the server returns a representation of the resource, often in JSON. The REST constraints favor stateless interactions, meaning each request must include all information necessary for processing; servers do not depend on prior requests to understand the current one. This statelessness makes APIs scalable and predictable in automation. A concrete example: when you request a list of users with a GET call to a users endpoint, the server responds with a JSON array describing each user. A common misconception is that REST requires a specific data format — it does not; JSON is conventional, but REST is an architectural style centered on uniform interface and stateless operations. For automation, this matters because you must select the correct HTTP verb: GET for retrieval, POST to create new entries, PUT to replace or update, and DELETE to remove. Choosing the wrong verb can cause errors or unexpected side effects. Key takeaway: think of endpoints as nouns and methods as verbs; that mental model helps you reason about safe interactions and prevents accidental data changes.

keyIdea.title: REST Grounding
keyIdea.text: REST focuses on stateless resource manipulation using standard HTTP verbs; understanding that model helps you design safe automation calls.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Definition
RESTful API — core idea
An API that uses HTTP methods against resource endpoints and keeps each request stateless.
Key properties
  • Uniform interface using HTTP verbs
  • Resources represented by endpoints and data formats like JSON
  • Stateless requests for scalability and simplicity
Concrete example
A GET request to a users endpoint returns a list of user objects. A POST to the same endpoint can create a new user with a JSON body like name and email.
Key Takeaway

Treat endpoints as nouns and HTTP methods as the verbs that act on them. This mental model prevents accidental writes when you intend to read.

Common misconception
Some learners assume REST enforces JSON only. In reality REST is about constraints; JSON is a widely used representation but not a requirement.
Analogy
Think of an API as a mail service: endpoints are mailboxes and HTTP methods are instructions like deliver, retrieve, or remove.
Why it matters for automation
  • Correct verbs avoid unintended changes.
  • Stateless calls are easier to retry and scale.
  • Clear contract via endpoints reduces debugging time.

screens.title: HTTP Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
screens.narratorSegment: HTTP methods, sometimes called verbs, are the primary way you express intent to a web service. GET asks the server to return a representation of a resource; it should be safe and idempotent, meaning repeated GETs do not change state. POST sends data to create a resource; multiple identical POSTs may create multiple resources unless the A P I de-duplicates. PUT is commonly used to update or replace an existing resource; it can be idempotent because repeating a PUT typically results in the same resource state. DELETE removes a resource. A concrete example: fetching a list of users uses GET, creating a new user uses POST with a JSON body, updating a user's profile uses PUT with the new fields, and removing a user uses DELETE. A common pitfall is accidentally using POST when you meant to update; this can create duplicate entries. In automation, pick the verb that matches the A P I documentation and test with a sandbox endpoint when possible. When writing scripts, document which endpoints are read-only and which change state. As a final check, run safe GET calls first to validate the returned structure before issuing POST or PUT that modify data.

keyIdea.title: Verb Choice
keyIdea.text: Use GET to read, POST to create, PUT to update or replace, and DELETE to remove; verb selection prevents unintended side effects.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Core Concept
HTTP Methods at a glance
GET — Retrieve resource representations. Safe and usually cacheable.
POST — Create a new resource. Include JSON payloads in the body.
PUT — Update or replace an existing resource. Often idempotent.
DELETE — Remove a resource. Check permissions before calling.
Step example
To add a user: send a POST to /users with a JSON body like name and email. Verify the server responded with 201 Created, then GET the new record to confirm.
Common mistakes
  • Using POST instead of PUT for updates, causing duplicate resources.
  • Not checking idempotency expectations; retries can create duplicates.
  • Assuming GET never fails; always check status codes and handle errors.
Pro Tip

When in doubt, consult the API docs and test against a sandbox endpoint. Document intent in your scripts.

screens.title: Using requests: basic calls and the json parameter
screens.narratorSegment: The requests library lets you make HTTP calls with simple, readable functions. The requests. get function sends a GET request and returns a Response object containing status_code, headers, and body. For POST or PUT operations you often want to send JSON; the json parameter accepts a Python dictionary, serializes it to JSON, and sets the Content-Type header automatically. A concrete example: using a POST to create a new item, you pass json={'name': 'New Item', 'quantity': 10} and include a timeout to prevent hanging. After the call, check response. status_code to confirm success, and call response. json() to parse the returned JSON. A frequent misconception is that response. json always succeeds; in practice you should verify the Content-Type header or handle JSONDecodeError because some endpoints may return empty bodies or non-JSON error messages. When writing automation, wrap calls in try-except to catch network errors and timeouts. We'll show starter code that follows these steps and demonstrates status checking, parsing, and basic error handling. Using requests: basic calls and the json parameter means use the json parameter to send payloads, inspect response.status_code and response.json, and always include timeouts and error handling.. In practical terms, how requests.get and requests.post handle data and headers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use the json parameter to send payloads, inspect response.status_code and response.json, and always include timeouts and error handling.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Process Flow
Code walkthrough
Starter pattern for POST with a timeout and error handling.
import requests

api_url = "https://api.example.com/items"
payload = {"name": "New Item", "quantity": 10}

try:
  response = requests.post(api_url, json=payload, timeout=5)
  response.raise_for_status()
  print("Item created", response.status_code)
  data = response.json()
  print("Response data:", data)
except requests.exceptions.Timeout:
  print("The request timed out after 5 seconds.")
except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
  print("An error occurred:", e)
Explanation & bullets
  • The json parameter serializes the payload and sets Content-Type automatically.
  • timeout prevents indefinite blocking of your script when the server is slow.
  • response.raise_for_status raises for 4xx and 5xx responses so errors surface immediately.
  • Always handle requests.exceptions.RequestException as a catch-all for network errors.
Key Takeaway

Use the json argument for payloads, set timeouts, and call raise_for_status to make failures explicit.

screens.title: Understanding Responses: status_code, headers, and body
screens.narratorSegment: When a server responds to your request it provides three main pieces of information: the status code, headers, and an optional body. The status code is a three-digit number that summarizes the server's result: codes in the 200 range indicate success, 201 is common for resource creation, 400-range codes represent client-side issues like bad requests or unauthorized access, and 500-range codes indicate server failures. In automation, always check response. status_code or use raise_for_status to convert error responses into exceptions you can handle. Headers provide metadata such as Content-Type, caching directives, or rate-limit counters; reading headers helps you decide whether to parse JSON or handle redirects. The response body contains the actual content, often JSON for APIs. Use response. json() to parse JSON into Python types but guard against JSON decoding errors if the server returns non-JSON error pages. A misconception is assuming a 200 status always means the content is valid; always validate structure after parsing. Example: after GETting a list of users, check that the returned object is a list and contains expected keys before using the data. This reduces runtime errors and makes automation robust.

keyIdea.text: Check status codes and headers before trusting the body. Parse JSON carefully and validate structure to avoid runtime errors.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Definition
Response anatomy
Status code: three-digit outcome like 200, 201, 404, 500.
Headers: key-value metadata; Content-Type indicates JSON vs HTML.
Body: the payload; often JSON when working with APIs.
Quick validation steps
  1. Check response.status_code or call raise_for_status.
  2. Confirm Content-Type includes application/json before calling response.json().
  3. Validate the data structure matches expectations (list vs dict and required keys).
Example scenario
You GET /users and receive 200 with Content-Type application/json. Call response.json(), inspect first element to confirm it has name and email keys before using them.
Common Mistake

Calling response.json() without checking Content-Type can raise exceptions if the server returned HTML or an empty body.

screens.title: Error handling: timeouts, exceptions, and raise_for_status
screens.narratorSegment: Network calls are inherently unreliable, so robust error handling is essential in automation. The requests library exposes specific exception types to help you respond to different problems. Always set a timeout to bound how long a call can block; for example, passing timeout=5 ensures the call fails fast if the server doesn't respond. Wrap requests calls in a try-except block and catch requests. exceptions. Timeout specifically for timeouts, and requests. exceptions. RequestException for other network or HTTP errors. Use response. raise_for_status to convert 4xx and 5xx HTTP responses into HTTPError exceptions so your script can handle them the same way as other failures. A concrete example: when posting data, catch Timeout to retry or log a message, catch HTTPError to inspect response. status_code and error body for debugging, and catch RequestException for DNS or connection issues. A common misconception is relying solely on status codes without catching network exceptions; that leads to unhandled crashes when the network itself fails. Finally, consider retry logic with backoff for transient failures but avoid infinite retries—limit retries and log failures so they can be investigated. This approach keeps automation predictable and easier to debug.

keyIdea.title: Handle Failures
keyIdea.text: Set timeouts, use try-except for specific requests exceptions, and call raise_for_status to surface HTTP errors for consistent handling.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Process Flow
Error handling patterns
Timeouts: pass timeout to prevent indefinite waits.
Specific exceptions: handle Timeout and RequestException separately.
raise_for_status: convert HTTP errors into exceptions to centralize error handling.
Example flow
  1. Try the request with a timeout.
  2. If it times out, log and optionally retry with backoff.
  3. If raise_for_status raises, inspect status_code and body to decide next steps.
Practical tips
  • Use short timeouts for user-facing scripts, longer for backend retries.
  • Log response.request.headers and response.text when debugging authorization or payload issues.
  • Avoid logging secrets; redact API keys when printing headers.
Check Your Understanding

If your script receives a timeout, what are two sensible next steps? Answer: log the event and consider a limited retry with backoff or surface the failure to user/monitoring.

screens.title: Authentication patterns: API keys and Basic Auth
screens.narratorSegment: Authentication lets an A P I verify who is calling it and whether that caller has permission for the requested operation. Common patterns include A P I keys and basic authentication. An A P I key is typically a token you send in an Authorization header, often prefixed with the word Bearer, or in a custom header or query parameter as the A P I documentation specifies. Basic authentication encodes a username and password in the Authorization header; the requests library supports basic auth via the auth helper so you don't manually construct headers. The critical security guidance is to never hardcode keys or passwords in source files. Instead, store credentials in environment variables or secure configuration stores, then read them at runtime. A common misconception is that HTTPS alone makes it safe to store keys in plain code — while HTTPS encrypts transport, hardcoded keys expose secrets in version control and to anyone with repo access. Example practice: export an A P I key into an environment variable and read it in your script to set headers for calls. This keeps secrets out of the codebase and reduces risk of accidental leakage.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Core Concept
Authentication patterns
API keys: token sent in Authorization header or a custom header, often Bearer tokens.
Basic auth: username and password encoded; use requests' auth helper for convenience.
Secure storage
Store keys outside code using environment variables or secure config. Load them at runtime to avoid accidental exposure in version control.
Example header
Set headers = {'Authorization': 'Bearer YOUR_API_KEY'} and pass headers=headers to requests calls. Replace YOUR_API_KEY with the value read from an environment variable at runtime.
Common Mistake

Hardcoding API keys in scripts exposes them to anyone with repository access. Use environment variables or secrets managers instead.

screens.title: Session objects and when to use them
screens.narratorSegment: Requests sessions provide a lightweight way to persist certain parameters across multiple requests. A Session object allows you to reuse headers, cookies, and TCP connections, which leads to performance benefits and cleaner code when you make many calls to the same host. For example, setting session. headers. update({'Authorization': 'Bearer...'}) lets subsequent session. get and session. post calls automatically include the authorization token. Sessions also maintain cookies from responses, which is useful for APIs that use session cookies rather than tokens. Another practical advantage is connection pooling: reusing the same session keeps sockets open for multiple requests, reducing latency. A misconception is that sessions magically handle all authentication flows; in reality, you still manage tokens and expiry logic. Use sessions for related requests in a workflow, and be explicit about closing a session when finished. In automation scripts, consider a session per worker or per logical operation to balance reuse and isolation. The payoff is more efficient network use and clearer code where common headers and behaviors are centralized. Session objects and when to use them means use a session to persist headers and cookies and to benefit from connection pooling when making multiple related requests.. In practical terms, maintain headers, cookies, and connection pooling across requests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Hands-on Activity
Starter code
import requests
import csv
import os

API_URL = "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users"
TARGET_CITY = "Gwenborough"

def create_output_dir(directory):
  if not os.path.exists(directory):
    os.makedirs(directory)

try:
  response = requests.get(API_URL, timeout=5)
  response.raise_for_status()
  users = response.json()
  for u in users:
    name = u.get('name')
    email = u.get('email')
    city = u.get('address', {}).get('city')
    print(name, email, city)
except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
  print("Request failed:", e)
Notes & tips
  • Check address exists before reading city to avoid KeyError.
  • Normalize city names before filtering to handle case differences.
  • Create output directory before writing CSV to prevent write errors.
Key Takeaway

This exercise combines request patterns, JSON parsing, and file output—core skills for automation that integrates API data.

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting steps
screens.narratorSegment: When A P I calls fail, a methodical troubleshooting approach will save time. Common errors include missing authentication leading to 401 or 403 responses, incorrect HTTP verb causing unexpected behavior, timeouts when the server is slow, and parsing errors when the response is not valid JSON. Start by inspecting response. status_code and response. text or response. headers; these often contain clear error messages or hints about required headers and content types. If you receive a 403 Forbidden, verify that the A P I key is present, not expired, and has appropriate permissions. A useful debugging step is to print response. request. headers to confirm what your client actually sent. Use tools like curl or Postman to replicate requests outside your script to rule out client-side code issues. When debugging timeouts, try a longer timeout locally to observe the server's behavior, then decide if retries or backoff are appropriate. Avoid excessive retries for 4xx responses; these usually indicate client mistakes. Logging structured errors and response contexts makes reproducing and fixing issues easier. This troubleshooting discipline reduces time spent chasing intermittent failures and helps you write more resilient automation.

Common errors

screens.title: Best practices for secure, maintainable API automation
screens.narratorSegment: Good practices keep your automation safe and maintainable. First, never hardcode secrets: use environment variables or configuration files that are excluded from version control. Second, always consult A P I documentation to learn endpoint requirements, allowed methods, and expected payloads; that prevents many common errors. Third, prefer idempotent operations where possible so retries won't create duplicates—PUT and DELETE have idempotent semantics that help here. Fourth, centralize repeated request behavior in functions or session objects to reduce duplicated header and timeout code. Fifth, add structured logging that records status codes and non-sensitive response details so you can trace failures without leaking secrets. A misconception is assuming short scripts do not need these safeguards; even small automation can run in CI or production and expose credentials if not protected. Finally, when saving A P I results to files, validate data before writing and handle file input and output errors gracefully. These practices reduce risk, improve observability, and make your A P I integrations reliable as they scale. In practical terms, store secrets safely, read docs, and make idempotent operations when possible. Web services and APIs are the bridges that let programs speak to cloud platforms, microservices, and external tools. In this lesson you will learn the core HTTP methods used to request, create, update, and delete resources, and you will see how the requests library makes those operations concise and readable. We'll cover how to read a response: the status code that tells you success or failure, headers that carry metadata, and JSON payloads that contain the actual data. You'll also learn practical error handling patterns: setting timeouts so scripts don't hang, using raise_for_status to detect HTTP errors, and catching network exceptions. Finally, we'll look at authentication patterns such as A P I keys and basic auth, and simple session usage for repeated requests. By the end you will be able to fetch data from a test A P I, inspect the response, and safely include credentials without embedding them directly in code. Notice why each step matters: understanding status codes avoids silent failures; proper authentication prevents rejected requests; and timeouts save automation from stalling. Ready to begin exploring these key topics with examples and starter code.

These objectives are practical skills you will practice during the chapter. First, you'll learn the meaning and appropriate use of common HTTP methods such as GET for retrieving data, POST for creating resources, PUT for updating, and DELETE for removal. We'll pair each verb with concrete examples so you can choose the right action when calling an A P I. Second, you'll use the requests library to make requests, pass JSON payloads, and inspect responses programmatically. That includes using the json parameter to serialize data and reading response. json to parse returned data. Third, you will learn to interpret HTTP status codes and response headers so you can detect success, client errors, or server errors and respond accordingly. Finally, you'll practice basic authentication patterns and safe credential handling by using headers, environment variables, or the requests auth helpers. Each objective is framed so you can immediately apply it in an automation script or debugging session.

In practice, these learning goals translate into repeatable tasks you will perform in automation scripts. You will construct a GET request to fetch JSON, check the status code, and safely parse the payload into Python data structures. You will write a POST call with a JSON body to create a new resource and set an explicit timeout to avoid waits that never end. You will interpret common error responses, using raise_for_status to surface HTTP errors and catching exceptions like timeouts and connection errors. Finally, you will practice attaching credentials to requests either with the auth helper for basic authentication or by adding an Authorization header for token-based access. Each objective matters because automation that assumes success without checks will behave unpredictably in production. By the end you'll be able to run small scripts against test APIs and export results confidently, knowing you handled errors and kept secrets secure.

A RESTful A P I is an interface that follows representational state transfer constraints, where clients interact with server-hosted resources via standard HTTP methods. In simple terms, an A P I exposes endpoints that represent data or services; you make requests and the server returns a representation of the resource, often in JSON. The REST constraints favor stateless interactions, meaning each request must include all information necessary for processing; servers do not depend on prior requests to understand the current one. This statelessness makes APIs scalable and predictable in automation. A concrete example: when you request a list of users with a GET call to a users endpoint, the server responds with a JSON array describing each user. A common misconception is that REST requires a specific data format — it does not; JSON is conventional, but REST is an architectural style centered on uniform interface and stateless operations. For automation, this matters because you must select the correct HTTP verb: GET for retrieval, POST to create new entries, PUT to replace or update, and DELETE to remove. Choosing the wrong verb can cause errors or unexpected side effects. Key takeaway: think of endpoints as nouns and methods as verbs; that mental model helps you reason about safe interactions and prevents accidental data changes.

HTTP methods, sometimes called verbs, are the primary way you express intent to a web service. GET asks the server to return a representation of a resource; it should be safe and idempotent, meaning repeated GETs do not change state. POST sends data to create a resource; multiple identical POSTs may create multiple resources unless the A P I de-duplicates. PUT is commonly used to update or replace an existing resource; it can be idempotent because repeating a PUT typically results in the same resource state. DELETE removes a resource. A concrete example: fetching a list of users uses GET, creating a new user uses POST with a JSON body, updating a user's profile uses PUT with the new fields, and removing a user uses DELETE. A common pitfall is accidentally using POST when you meant to update; this can create duplicate entries. In automation, pick the verb that matches the A P I documentation and test with a sandbox endpoint when possible. When writing scripts, document which endpoints are read-only and which change state. As a final check, run safe GET calls first to validate the returned structure before issuing POST or PUT that modify data.

The requests library lets you make HTTP calls with simple, readable functions. The requests. get function sends a GET request and returns a Response object containing status_code, headers, and body. For POST or PUT operations you often want to send JSON; the json parameter accepts a Python dictionary, serializes it to JSON, and sets the Content-Type header automatically. A concrete example: using a POST to create a new item, you pass json={'name': 'New Item', 'quantity': 10} and include a timeout to prevent hanging. After the call, check response. status_code to confirm success, and call response. json() to parse the returned JSON. A frequent misconception is that response. json always succeeds; in practice you should verify the Content-Type header or handle JSONDecodeError because some endpoints may return empty bodies or non-JSON error messages. When writing automation, wrap calls in try-except to catch network errors and timeouts. We'll show starter code that follows these steps and demonstrates status checking, parsing, and basic error handling. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When a server responds to your request it provides three main pieces of information: the status code, headers, and an optional body. The status code is a three-digit number that summarizes the server's result: codes in the 200 range indicate success, 201 is common for resource creation, 400-range codes represent client-side issues like bad requests or unauthorized access, and 500-range codes indicate server failures. In automation, always check response. status_code or use raise_for_status to convert error responses into exceptions you can handle. Headers provide metadata such as Content-Type, caching directives, or rate-limit counters; reading headers helps you decide whether to parse JSON or handle redirects. A misconception is assuming a 200 status always means the content is valid; always validate structure after parsing. Network calls are inherently unreliable, so robust error handling is essential in automation. The requests library exposes specific exception types to help you respond to different problems. Always set a timeout to bound how long a call can block; for example, passing timeout=5 ensures the call fails fast if the server doesn't respond. A common misconception is relying solely on status codes without catching network exceptions; that leads to unhandled crashes when the network itself fails. Finally, consider retry logic with backoff for transient failures but avoid infinite retries—limit retries and log failures so they can be investigated. This approach keeps automation predictable and easier to debug.

Authentication lets an A P I verify who is calling it and whether that caller has permission for the requested operation. Common patterns include A P I keys and basic authentication. An A P I key is typically a token you send in an Authorization header, often prefixed with the word Bearer, or in a custom header or query parameter as the A P I documentation specifies.
